Section A: Bone Tissue and the Skeletal SystemPart 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: And now on to Part 1. The Functions of the Skeletal System.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Size & shape of bones related to function
Bones (osseus tissue) all are dynamic living tissue, with growth, repair, renewal:
modify strength and thickness in responses to changes in muscle size and body weight
gain and lose minerals as part of homeostasis

Left femur of extinct elephant. Credit: See page for author, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
From visits to museums, and seeing fossilized bones of extinct animals, it’s easy to think of bones as static. However, your skeleton is a structure of living tissue that grows, repairs, and renews itself. The bones within it are dynamic and complex organs that serve a number of important functions, including helping to maintain homeostasis of a number of substances.

The skeletal system forms the rigid internal framework of the body. It consists of the bones, cartilages, and ligaments. Bones, or osseous tissue, support the weight of the body, allow for body movements, and protect internal organs. Cartilage provides flexible strength and support for body structures such as the thoracic cage, the external ear, and the trachea and larynx. At joints of the body, cartilage can also unite adjacent bones or provide cushioning between them. Ligaments are the strong connective tissue bands that hold the bones at a moveable joint together and serve to prevent excessive movements of the joint that would result in injury. Providing movement of the skeleton are the muscles of the body, which are firmly attached to the skeleton via connective tissue structures called tendons. As muscles contract, they pull on the bones to produce movements of the body. 

Each bone of the body serves a particular function, and therefore bones vary in size, shape, and strength based on these functions. For example, the bones of the lower back and lower limb are thick and strong to support your body weight. Similarly, the size of a bony landmark that serves as a muscle attachment site on an individual bone is related to the strength of this muscle. Muscles can apply very strong pulling forces to the bones of the skeleton. To resist these forces, bones have enlarged bony landmarks at sites where powerful muscles attach. This means that not only the size of a bone, but also its shape, is related to its function. Bones are also dynamic organs that can modify their strength and thickness in response to changes in muscle strength or body weight. 

Thus, muscle attachment sites on bones will thicken if you begin a workout program that increases muscle strength. Similarly, the walls of weight-bearing bones will thicken if you gain body weight or begin a new running regimen. In contrast, a reduction in muscle strength or body weight will cause bones to become thinner. This may happen during a prolonged hospital stay, following limb immobilization in a cast, or going into the weightlessness of outer space. Even a change in diet, such as eating only soft food due to the loss of teeth, will result in a noticeable decrease in the size and thickness of the jaw bones.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Skeletal system consists of more than just bones: 
bones
cartilages
ligaments
tendons
Various functions, including…

Joint. Credit: Madhero88, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Bone, or osseous tissue, is a hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton, the support structure of the body. In the areas of the skeleton where bones move (for example, the ribcage and joints), cartilage, a semi-rigid form of connective tissue, provides flexibility and smooth surfaces for movement. The skeletal system is the body system composed of bones, cartilages, and ligaments.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Support
skeleton is scaffold for body

Projectional rendering of CT scan of thorax. Credit: Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Beams under the roof of Musée d'Orsay. Credit: Ivonna Nowicka, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Support

The most apparent functions of the skeletal system are the gross functions—those visible by regular observation. Simply by looking at a person, you can see how the bones support, facilitate movement, and protect the human body.

Just as the steel beams of a building provide a scaffold to support its weight, the bones and cartilage of your skeletal system compose the scaffold that supports the rest of your body. Without the skeletal system, you would be a limp mass of organs, muscle, and skin.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Movement
bones serve as attachment points for muscles
bones act as levers, with joints serving as fulcrums

Third-class lever.

Third-class lever as seen in the body. (credit: sarahmckinnon/flickr.com)

Bones Support Movement. Bones act as levers when muscles span a joint and contract. (credit: Benjamin J. DeLong)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Movement

Bones also facilitate movement by serving as points of attachment for your muscles. While some bones only serve as a support for the muscles, others also transmit the forces produced when your muscles contract. From a mechanical point of view, bones act as levers and joints serve as fulcrums. Unless a muscle spans a joint and contracts, a bone is not going to move. We’ll explain these concepts in more detail in the Biomechanics unit.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Protection
bones protect internal organs from injury

Projectional rendering of CT scan of thorax. Credit: Mikael Häggström, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Bones Protect the Brain. The cranium completely surrounds and protects the brain from non-traumatic injury.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Protection

Bones protect internal organs from injury by covering or surrounding them. For example, your ribs protect your lungs and heart, the bones of your vertebral column (also called your spine) protect your spinal cord, and the bones of your cranium (also called your skull) protect your brain.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Mineral Storage
reservoir for calcium, phosphorus, and other minerals
aids in maintenance of mineral homeostasis
e.g., parathyroid hormone (PTH) aids in calcium homeostasis

Calcium Level Regulation. Adapted from: Mkaram19, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Mineral Storage

On a metabolic level, bone tissue performs several critical functions. For one, the bone matrix (the ground substance of bones) acts as a reservoir for a number of minerals important to the functioning of the body, especially calcium, and phosphorus. These minerals, incorporated into bone tissue to provide hardness, can be released back into the bloodstream to maintain levels needed to support physiological processes. Calcium ions, for example, are essential for muscle contractions and controlling the flow of other ions involved in the transmission of nerve impulses. Parathyroid hormone, abbreviated PTH and shown in this diagram, is just one of the ways in which the body regulates calcium homeostasis.

slides.title: Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System
slides.body:
Part 1: The Functions of the Skeletal System

Energy Storage, and Hematopoiesis
site for fat storage: yellow marrow adipose tissue (with triglycerides)
site for blood cell production: red marrow is site of hematopoiesis (production of blood cells):
red blood cells 
white blood cells
platelets

Head of the Femur Showing Red and Yellow Marrow. The head of the femur contains both yellow and red marrow. Yellow marrow stores fat. Red marrow is responsible for hematopoiesis. (credit: modification of work by “stevenfruitsmaak”/Wikimedia Commons)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Energy Storage, and Hematopoiesis

Bone also serves as a site for fat storage and blood cell production. The softer connective tissue that fills the interior of most bone is referred to as bone marrow. There are two types of bone marrow: yellow marrow and red marrow. Yellow marrow contains adipose tissue; the triglycerides stored in the adipocytes of the tissue can serve as a source of energy. Red marrow is the site of hematopoiesis—the production of blood cells. Red blood cells, white blood cells, and cell fragments called platelets are all produced in the red marrow.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

206 major bones in adult
5 main categories (based on shape)
(extra sutural bones are also present, plus we’re ignoring those here)

Bone Classification by Shape

Classifications of Bones. Bones can be classified according to their shape.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The 206 major bones that compose the adult skeleton can be divided into five categories based on their shapes. Their shapes and their functions are related such that each categorical shape of bone has a distinct function. Some sources also include a sixth category, sutural bones, which are extra bone pieces that can occur within a suture of the skull, but we will not address those here. Because of such occasional extra bones within the sutures or elsewhere, your body likely contains more that 206 bones, but the 206 represents the major bones that are usually present.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

Long Bones
cylindrical in shape
diameter smaller than its height
function as levers (move, when muscles contract)

Long bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Tibia. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Long bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes: Long Bones: A long bone is one that is cylindrical in shape, with a diameter smaller than its height. Keep in mind, however, that the term describes the shape of a bone, not its size. Long bones are found in the arms (humerus, ulna, and radius) and legs (femur, tibia, and fibula), as well as in the hands (metacarpals and phalanges) and feet (metatarsals and phalanges). Long bones function as levers; they move when muscles contract.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

Short Bones
cube-like (approximately equal in length, width, and thickness)
provide stability and 			             limited motion

Short bones. Adapted from: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Tarsus (tarsal bones). Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Short bones. Adapted from: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes: Short Bones: A short bone is one that is cube-like in shape, being approximately equal in length, width, and thickness. The only short bones in the human skeleton are in the carpals of the wrists and the tarsals of the ankles. Short bones provide stability and support as well as some limited motion.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

Flat bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Flat Bones
thin, but also often curved
serve as points of attachment for muscles 
protect internal organs

Flat bones of skull. Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Flat bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes: Flat Bones: The term “flat bone” is somewhat of a misnomer because, although a flat bone is typically thin, it is also often curved. Examples include the cranial bones of the skull, the scapulae (shoulder blades), the sternum (breastbone), and the ribs. Flat bones serve as points of attachment for muscles and often protect internal organs.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

Irregular bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Irregular Bones
complex shapes
shapes do not fit other classifications
protect from compression (e.g., vertebrae)
contain sinuses (spaces; e.g., facial bones)

Irregular bones of skull. Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Irregular bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes: Irregular Bones: An irregular bone is one that does not have any easily characterized shape and therefore does not fit any other classification. These bones tend to have more complex shapes, like the vertebrae that support the spinal cord and protect it from compressive forces. Many facial bones, particularly the ones containing sinuses, are classified as irregular bones.

slides.title: Part 2: Bone Classification
slides.body:
Part 2: Bone Classification

Sesamoid Bones
small, round (like sesame seed)
form in tendons, counter compression, increases leverage by sticking out and increasing angle
numbers vary by person
but most everyone
    has patellae

Sesamoid bones. Adapted from: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Patella. Credit: Pearson Scott Foresman, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Sesamoid bones. Adapted from: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes: Sesamoid Bones: A sesamoid bone is a small, round bone that, as the name suggests, is shaped like a sesame seed. These bones form in tendons (the sheaths of tissue that connect bones to muscles) where a great deal of pressure is generated in a joint. The sesamoid bones protect tendons by helping them overcome compressive forces. Sesamoid bones vary in number and placement from person to person but are typically found in tendons associated with the feet, hands, and knees. The patellae (singular = patella) are the only sesamoid bones found commonly in every person.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Gross Anatomy of Bone
diaphysis (tubular shaft)
medullary cavity (hollow region)
yellow marrow
compact bone walls
epiphysis (wide ends)
 spongy bone 
red marrow
metaphysis
epiphyseal plate (growth plate)
layer of hyaline cartilage
cartilage replaced by osseous tissue and the epiphyseal plate becomes an epiphyseal line when growth stops

Anatomy of a Long Bone. A typical long bone shows the gross anatomical characteristics of bone.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Gross Anatomy of Bone

The structure of a long bone allows for the best visualization of all of the parts of a bone. A long bone has two parts: the diaphysis and the epiphysis.

The diaphysis is the tubular shaft that runs between the proximal and distal ends of the bone. The hollow region in the diaphysis is called the medullary cavity, which is filled with yellow marrow. The walls of the diaphysis are composed of dense and hard compact bone. 

The wider section at each end of the bone is called the epiphysis (plural = epiphyses), which is filled with spongy bone. Red marrow fills the spaces in the spongy bone.

Each epiphysis meets the diaphysis at the metaphysis, the narrow area that contains the epiphyseal plate (which is also called the growth plate), a layer of hyaline cartilage in a growing bone. When the bone stops growing in early adulthood (approximately 18–21 years of age), the cartilage is replaced by osseous tissue and the epiphyseal plate becomes an epiphyseal line.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Gross Anatomy of Bone
endosteum (cellular inner lining of medullary cavity and trabeculae)
bone growth, repair, and remodeling
periosteum (outer surface of bone)
contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels 
inner cellular layer involved in bone growth, repair, and remodeling
outer fibrous layer is attachment point for tendons and ligaments
replaced by articular (hyaline) cartilage (to reduce friction) where bones meet to form joints

Periosteum and Endosteum. The periosteum forms the outer surface of bone, and the endosteum lines the internal surfaces of bone, like the medullary cavity.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The medullary cavity has a cellular layer of delicate membranous lining called the endosteum (end- meaning “inside” and oste- meaning “bone”), where bone growth, repair, and remodeling occur. The endosteum is also found along the trabeculae of spongy bone. The outer surface of the bone is covered with a membrane called the periosteum (peri– meaning “around” or “surrounding”). The periosteum contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels that nourish compact bone. The periosteum contains an inner cellular layer also participates in bone growth, repair, and remodeling. An outer fibrous layer serves as an attachment point for tendons and ligaments. The periosteum covers the entire outer surface except where the epiphyses meet other bones to form joints. In this region, the epiphyses are covered with articular cartilage, a thin layer of cartilage that reduces friction and acts as a shock absorber.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Gross Anatomy of Bone
flat bones consist of a layer of spongy bone (also called diploë), lined on either side by a layer of compact bone
double protection: if outer layer cracked, brain is still protected by inner layer

Anatomy of a Flat Bone. This cross-section of a flat bone shows the spongy bone (diploë) lined on either side by a layer of compact bone.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Flat bones, like those of the cranium, consist of a layer of spongy bone (also called diploë), lined on either side by a layer of compact bone. The two layers of compact bone and the interior spongy bone work together to protect the internal organs. If the outer layer of a cranial bone fractures, the brain is still protected by the intact inner layer.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Bone Cells and Tissue
matrix:
hydroxyapatite
mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate 
calcification forms on collagen fibres
salt crystals give hardness
fibres give flexibility

SEM of heat-treated hydroxyapatite coatings. Credit: Ahmed E. Hannora, Alexander S. Mukasyan, Zulkhair A. Mansurov, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Bone Cells and Tissue

Bone contains a relatively small number of cells entrenched in a matrix of collagen fibres that provide a surface for inorganic salt crystals to adhere. These salt crystals, made of a substance called hydroxyapatite, form when calcium phosphate and calcium carbonate combine with other inorganic salts and solidify, (i.e. calcify) on the collagen fibres. The crystals give bones their hardness and strength, while the collagen fibres give them flexibility so that they are not brittle.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Bone Cells and Tissue
bone cells:
osteoblasts
found in growing bone
incl. periosteum and endosteum
secrete matrix to form new bone
when sealed in matrix, become osteocyte
osteocytes
primary cell of mature bone
maintain mineral concentration of matrix
located in a space called a lacuna
get nutrients via canaliculi channels 
(see slide 28 for image of lacunae and canaliculi)

Bone Cells. Four types of cells are found within bone tissue. Osteogenic cells are undifferentiated and develop into osteoblasts. When osteoblasts get trapped within the calcified matrix, their structure and function changes, and they become osteocytes. Osteoclasts develop from monocytes and macrophages and differ in appearance from other bone cells.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Although bone cells comprise a small amount of the bone volume, relative to the matrix, they are crucial to the function of bones. Four types of cells are found within bone tissue: osteoblasts, osteocytes, osteogenic cells, and osteoclasts.

The osteoblast is the bone cell responsible for forming new bone and is found in the growing portions of bone, including the periosteum and endosteum. Osteoblasts do not divide; instead, they synthesize and secrete the collagen matrix and calcium salts. As the secreted matrix surrounding the osteoblast calcifies, the osteoblast become trapped within it; as a result, it changes in structure and becomes an osteocyte, the most common type of bone cell. Each osteocyte is located in a space called a lacuna and is surrounded by bone matrix. Osteocytes maintain the mineral concentration of the matrix. Like osteoblasts, osteocytes lack mitotic division activity. They can communicate with each other and receive nutrients via long cytoplasmic processes that extend through canaliculi, channels within the bone matrix.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Bone Cells and Tissue
bone cells:
osteogenic cells
only bone cells that can undergo mitosis
in the deep layers of the periosteum and the marrow 
produce new osteoblasts
osteoclasts
bone breakdown & resorption
multinucleated
originate from monocytes and macrophages (not osteogenic cell)
bones constantly remodeled
constantly breaking down bone, while osteoblasts build bone

Bone Cells. Four types of cells are found within bone tissue. Osteogenic cells are undifferentiated and develop into osteoblasts. When osteoblasts get trapped within the calcified matrix, their structure and function changes, and they become osteocytes. Osteoclasts develop from monocytes and macrophages and differ in appearance from other bone cells.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Neither osteoblasts, nor osteocytes are capable of mitosis, and thus cannot divide. They are thus constantly replenished by osteogenic cells. These osteogenic cells are undifferentiated with high mitotic activity and they are the only bone cells that divide. Immature osteogenic cells are found in the deep layers of the periosteum and the marrow. They differentiate and develop into osteoblasts.

The dynamic nature of bone means that new tissue is constantly formed, and old, injured, or unnecessary bone is dissolved for repair or for calcium release. The cell responsible for bone resorption, or breakdown, is the osteoclast. They are found on bone surfaces, are multinucleated, and originate from monocytes and macrophages, two types of white blood cells, not from osteogenic cells. Osteoclasts are continually breaking down old bone while osteoblasts are continually forming new bone. The ongoing balance between osteoblasts and osteoclasts is responsible for the constant but subtle reshaping of bone.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Compact Bone (vs. spongy)
a.k.a. cortical bone
denser & stronger
deep to periosteum (outer layer) & in diaphysis (middle) of long bones
osteon (individual unit)
lamellae: concentric calcified matrix rings
lacunae located between these
central canal
blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels
connects to lacunae via smaller canalliculi
central canal branches off at right angles through a perforating canal, to reach periosteum and endosteum

Compact Bone. This cross-sectional view of compact bone shows the basic structural unit, the osteon.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Compact versus Spongy Bone

The differences between compact and spongy bone are best explored via their histology. Most bones contain compact and spongy osseous tissue, but their distribution and concentration vary based on the bone’s overall function. Compact bone is dense so that it can withstand compressive forces, while spongy (or cancellous) bone has open spaces and supports shifts in weight distribution.

Let’s look first at compact bone. Compact bone is the denser, stronger of the two types of bone tissue. It can be found deep to the periosteum (the outer layer) and in the diaphyses (middle) of long bones, where it provides support and protection.

The microscopic structural unit of compact bone is called an osteon. Each osteon is composed of concentric rings of calcified matrix called lamellae. Running down the center of each osteon is the central canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, and lymphatic vessels. These vessels and nerves branch off at right angles through a perforating canal, to extend to the periosteum and endosteum.

The osteocytes are located inside spaces called lacunae, found at the borders of adjacent lamellae. As described earlier, canaliculi connect with the canaliculi of other lacunae and eventually with the central canal. This system allows nutrients to be transported to the osteocytes and wastes to be removed from them.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Spongy Bone (a.k.a., cancellous bone/trabecular bone)
osteocytes in lacunae, but within trabeculae, not osteons
lighter, making bones easier to move
spaces in some spongy bones contain red marrow – allows for hematopoiesis

Spongy Bone. Spongy bone is composed of trabeculae that contain the osteocytes. Red marrow fills the spaces in some bones.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Like compact bone, spongy bone, also known as cancellous bone, contains osteocytes housed in lacunae, but they are not arranged in concentric circles. Instead, the lacunae and osteocytes are found in a lattice-like network of matrix spikes called trabeculae. The trabeculae may appear to be a random network, but each trabecula forms along lines of stress to provide strength to the bone. The spaces of the trabeculated network provide balance to the dense and heavy compact bone by making bones lighter so that muscles can move them more easily. In addition, the spaces in some spongy bones contain red marrow, protected by the trabeculae, where hematopoiesis occurs.

slides.title: Part 3: Bone Structure
slides.body:
Part 3: Bone Structure

Blood and Nerve Supply
arteries and veins pass through the compact bone of diaphysis
through the nutrient foramen
smaller openings in spongy bone also allow access to blood vessels from periosteum 
nerves also enter through same openings
sense pain, regulate blood vessel dilation to shunt blood to metabolically active regions (e.g., regions of growth)

Blood and Nerve Supply to Bone. Blood vessels and nerves enter the bone through the nutrient foramen.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The spongy bone and medullary cavity receive nourishment from arteries that pass through the compact bone. The arteries enter through the nutrient foramen, a small opening in the diaphysis. The osteocytes in spongy bone are nourished by blood vessels of the periosteum that penetrate spongy bone and blood that circulates in the marrow cavities. As the blood passes through the marrow cavities, it is collected by veins, which then pass out of the bone through the same foramen.

In addition to the blood vessels, nerves follow the same paths into the bone where they tend to concentrate in the more metabolically active regions of the bone. The nerves sense pain, and it appears the nerves also play roles in regulating blood supplies and in bone growth, hence their concentrations in metabolically active sites of the bone.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We now turn to Part 4: Bone Formation and Development.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Cartilage Templates
bone is a replacement tissue that lays down its mineral matrix on other tissue, usually cartilage
cartilage matrix is secreted by chondroblasts, which when completely surrounded by matrix are called chondocytes
embryo (6th – 7th week) undergoes ossification (or osteogenesis):
intramembranous ossification 
endochondral ossification

Human Embryo (7th week of pregnancy, which includes 2-week pre-ovulatory follicular period, or 5th week post ovulation, which is near time of fertilization). Credit: Ed Uthman, MD (Flickr, Wikipedia), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Cartilage Templates

Bone is a replacement tissue; that is, it uses a model tissue on which to lay down its mineral matrix. For skeletal development, the most common template is cartilage. During fetal development, a framework is laid down that determines where bones will form. This framework is a flexible, semi-solid cartilage matrix produced by chondroblasts. As the matrix surrounds and isolates chondroblasts, they mature into cells called chondrocytes. 

Throughout fetal development and into childhood, bone forms on the cartilaginous matrix. By the time a fetus is born, most of the cartilage has been replaced with bone. Some additional cartilage will be replaced throughout childhood, and some cartilage remains in the adult skeleton.

The actual process of bone development, ossification (or osteogenesis), occurs via one of two osteogenic pathways—intramembranous ossification or endochondral ossification—but bone is the same regardless of the pathway that produces it.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Intramembranous Ossification
compact and spongy bone develops directly from undifferentiated (mesenchymal) connective tissue (not over cartilage)
cranial bones, flat bones of face, clavicles (collarbones)

Flat bones in skull. Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: During intramembranous ossification, compact and spongy bone develops directly from sheets of mesenchymal – that is, undifferentiated – connective tissue. The flat bones of the face, most of the cranial bones, and the clavicles (or collarbones) are initially formed via intramembranous ossification.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Intramembranous Ossification
mesenchymal (stem) cells gather in ossification center (later spreads out)
differentiate into capillaries and osteogenic cells which become osteoblasts
osteoblasts secrete osteoid (uncalcified matrix)
osteoid calcifies over days trapping osteoblasts, turning them into osteocytes
osteoid around capillaries becomes trabecular matrix; osteoblasts on surface of spongy bone become the periosteum
periosteum then creates a protective layer of compact bone superficial to the trabecular bone; blood vessels condense into red marrow

Intramembranous Ossification. Intramembranous ossification follows four steps. (a) Mesenchymal cells group into clusters, and ossification centers form. (b) Secreted osteoid traps osteoblasts, which then become osteocytes. (c) Trabecular matrix and periosteum form. (d) Compact bone develops superficial to the trabecular bone, and crowded blood vessels condense into red marrow.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The process begins when mesenchymal cells in the embryonic skeleton gather together and begin to differentiate into specialized cells (part a in the figure). Some of these cells will form capillaries, while others will become osteogenic cells and then osteoblasts. Although they will ultimately be spread out by the formation of bone tissue, early osteoblasts appear in a cluster called an ossification centre.

The osteoblasts secrete osteoid, uncalcified matrix, which calcifies within a few days as mineral salts are deposited on it, thereby trapping the osteoblasts within. Once entrapped, the osteoblasts become osteocytes (this is shown in part b of the figure). 

Osteoid secreted around the capillaries results in a trabecular matrix, while osteoblasts on the surface of the spongy bone become the periosteum (shown in part c of the figure). The periosteum then creates a protective layer of compact bone superficial to the trabecular bone. The trabecular bone crowds nearby blood vessels, which eventually condense into red marrow (shown in part d of the figure).

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Intramembranous Ossification
skeleton not fully ossified at birth
skull can thus deform to allow passage through birth canal
flat bones of cranium keep growing through childhood
ultimately fuse at immobile joints called sutures
last bones to ossify are flat bones of the face (grow larger and ossify during adolescence)

Newborn Skull. The bones of the newborn skull are not fully ossified and are separated by large areas called fontanelles, which are filled with fibrous connective tissue. The fontanelles allow for continued growth of the skull after birth. At the time of birth, the facial bones are small and underdeveloped, and the mastoid process has not yet formed.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Intramembranous ossification begins in utero during fetal development and continues on into adolescence. At birth, the skeleton is not fully ossified. Most joints of the skull, for example, are more mobile in an infant than an adult to allow the skull to deform during passage through the birth canal. The flat bones of the cranium continue to grow throughout childhood, ultimately being separated by narrow immobile joints called sutures. 

The last bones to ossify via intramembranous ossification are the flat bones of the face, which reach their adult size at the end of the adolescent growth spurt.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Endochondral Ossification
bone develops by replacing hyaline cartilage
takes much longer than intramembranous ossification
bones at the base of the skull and long bones

Irregular bones. Credit: BodyParts3D is made by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Long bones. Credit: Anatomography is provided by DBCLS, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: In endochondral ossification, bone develops by replacing hyaline cartilage. Cartilage does not become bone, but instead serves as a template to be completely replaced by new bone. Endochondral ossification takes much longer than intramembranous ossification. Bones at the base of the skull and long bones form via endochondral ossification.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Endochondral Ossification
mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts, which secrete cartilaginous matrix, and become chondrocytes
the perichondrium, a membrane that covers the cartilage, appears 
capillaries penetrate cartilage, carrying osteogenic cells, many of which differentiate into osteoblasts
perichondrium is now transformed into the periosteum
as matrix calcifies, nutrients no longer reach chondrocytes in the centre; they die and the surrounding cartilage disintegrates
blood vessels cause inner cavities to enlarge; cavities eventually combine to become the medullary cavity

Endochondral Ossification. Endochondral ossification follows five steps. (a) Mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts that secrete cartilage matrix to form a hyaline cartilage model of the future bony skeleton.  The perichondrium forms. (b) The cartilage model starts to calcify; chondrocytes begin to die and the cartilage begins to degenerate. (c) Periosteal bud penetrates cartilage of the diaphysis; the primary ossification center develops.  A bony collar develops around the diaphysis of the bone.  Perichondrium transforms into periosteum.  (d) Cartilage continue to grow at ends of the bone. Medullary cavity forms. (e) Periosteal buds penetrate cartilage at epiphyses; secondary ossification centers develop. (f) Cartilage remains at epiphyseal (growth) plate and at joint surface as articular cartilage.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In a long bone, for example, at about 6 to 8 weeks after conception, some of the mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts. The chondroblasts secrete the organic components of cartilage matrix that form the cartilaginous skeletal precursor of the bones (shown in part a of the figure). Once encased in the matrix, these cells are called chondrocytes. The perichondrium, a membrane that covers the cartilage, now also appears (show in parts a and b of the figure).

As the cartilage grows, capillaries penetrate it, carrying osteogenic cells with them, many of which will become osteoblasts. This penetration initiates the transformation of the perichondrium into the bone-producing periosteum, and a primary ossification center forms  (part c in the figure).

As the matrix calcifies, nutrients can no longer reach the chondrocytes in the centre of the cartilage model. This results in their death and the disintegration of the surrounding cartilage. The blood vessels cause the inner cavities to enlarge, and the cavities eventually combine to become the medullary cavity (part d in the figure).

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

Endochondral Ossification
chondrocytes and cartilage continue to grow at the ends of the bone (helping form epiphyses)
secondary ossification centres form here after birth
same sequence of events (matrix mineralization, chondrocyte death, invasion of blood vessels from periosteum, and seeding with osteogenic cells that become osteoblasts) occurs here
cartilage only remains at:
joint surface as articular cartilage 
between the diaphysis and epiphysis as the epiphyseal plate allowing for continued growth until sealed

Endochondral Ossification. Endochondral ossification follows five steps. (a) Mesenchymal cells differentiate into chondroblasts that secrete cartilage matrix to form a hyaline cartilage model of the future bony skeleton.  The perichondrium forms. (b) The cartilage model starts to calcify; chondrocytes begin to die and the cartilage begins to degenerate. (c) Periosteal bud penetrates cartilage of the diaphysis; the primary ossification center develops.  A bony collar develops around the diaphysis of the bone.  Perichondrium transforms into periosteum.  (d) Cartilage continue to grow at ends of the bone. Medullary cavity forms. (e) Periosteal buds penetrate cartilage at epiphyses; secondary ossification centers develop. (f) Cartilage remains at epiphyseal (growth) plate and at joint surface as articular cartilage.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
While these deep changes are occurring, chondrocytes and cartilage continue to grow at the ends of the bone (the future epiphyses), which increases the bone’s length at the same time bone is replacing cartilage in the diaphysis. By the time the fetal skeleton is fully formed, cartilage only remains at the joint surface as articular cartilage and between the diaphysis and epiphysis as the epiphyseal plate, the latter of which is responsible for the longitudinal growth of bones (you can see this plate in part f of the figure). 

After birth, this same sequence of events (matrix mineralization, death of chondrocytes, invasion of blood vessels from the periosteum, and seeding with osteogenic cells that become osteoblasts) occurs in the epiphyseal regions, and each of these centers of activity is referred to as a secondary ossification centre (shown in part e of the figure).

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

How bones grow in length:
epiphyseal plate - layer of hyaline cartilage where ossification occurs in long bones
cartilage formed on epiphyseal side
ossification on the diaphyseal side
reserve zone – chondrocytes in matrix: secure epiphyseal plate to osseous tissue of epiphysis
proliferative zone – new immature chondrocytes made (a.k.a., chondroblasts; via mitosis)
zone of maturation and hypertrophy – chondrocytes mature and enlarge
zone of calcified matrix – chondrocytes here are dead, osteoblasts from diaphysis cause calcification; forms connection to rest of calcified diaphysis

Bone Growth in Length. The epiphyseal plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
How Bones Grow in Length

The epiphyseal plate is the area of growth in a long bone. It is a layer of hyaline cartilage where ossification occurs in immature bones. On the epiphyseal side of the epiphyseal plate, cartilage is formed. On the diaphyseal side, cartilage is ossified, and the diaphysis grows in length. The epiphyseal plate is composed of four zones of cells and activity (shown in the figure). 

The reserve zone is the region closest to the epiphyseal end of the plate and contains small chondrocytes within the matrix. These chondrocytes do not participate in bone growth but secure the epiphyseal plate to the osseous tissue of the epiphysis.

The proliferative zone is the next layer toward the diaphysis and contains stacks of slightly larger chondrocytes. It makes new chondrocytes (via mitosis) to replace those that die at the diaphyseal end of the plate. 

Chondrocytes in the next layer, the zone of maturation and hypertrophy, are older and larger than those in the proliferative zone. The more mature cells are situated closer to the diaphyseal end of the plate. The longitudinal growth of bone is a result of cellular division in the proliferative zone and the maturation of cells in the zone of maturation and hypertrophy.

Most of the chondrocytes in the zone of calcified matrix, the zone closest to the diaphysis, are dead because the matrix around them has calcified. Capillaries and osteoblasts from the diaphysis penetrate this zone, and the osteoblasts secrete bone tissue on the remaining calcified cartilage.

Thus, the zone of calcified matrix connects the epiphyseal plate to the diaphysis. A bone grows in length when osseous tissue is added to the diaphysis.

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

How bones grow in length:
growth controlled by hormones
growth ends in early adulthood
chondrocytes proliferation ceases
bone replaces cartilage, leaving solely epiphyseal line (replaces epiphyseal plate)

Progression from Epiphyseal Plate to Epiphyseal Line. As a bone matures, the epiphyseal plate fully ossifies into an epiphyseal line. (a) Epiphyseal plates are visible in a growing bone. (b) Epiphyseal lines are the remnants of epiphyseal plates in a mature bone.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Bones continue to grow in length until early adulthood. The rate of growth is controlled by hormones, which will be discussed later. When the chondrocytes in the epiphyseal plate cease their proliferation and bone replaces the cartilage, longitudinal growth stops. All that remains of the epiphyseal plate is the now fully ossified epiphyseal line (as shown in this figure).

slides.title: Part 4: Bone Formation and Development
slides.body:
Part 4: Bone Formation and Development

How bones grow in diameter:
modeling process (during bone growth – erosion of old bone along medullary cavity & deposition of new bone beneath periosteum):
appositional growth (growth in diameter)
can continue even after longitudinal growth ceases
osteoclasts resorb old bone in medullary cavity
osteoblasts, via intramembranous ossification, produce new bone beneath periosteum
remodeling process (continuous, throughout adulthood):
in adulthood
resorption of old or damaged bone on same surface where new bone is laid
5-10% of skeleton remodeled annually 
extra remodeling due to injury, exercise, etc.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
How Bones Grow in Diameter

While bones are increasing in length, they are also increasing in diameter; growth in diameter can continue even after longitudinal growth ceases. This is called appositional growth. Osteoclasts resorb old bone that lines the medullary cavity, while osteoblasts, via intramembranous ossification, produce new bone tissue beneath the periosteum. The erosion of old bone along the medullary cavity and the deposition of new bone beneath the periosteum not only increase the diameter of the diaphysis but also increase the diameter of the medullary cavity. This process is called modeling.

The process in which matrix is resorbed on one surface of a bone and deposited on another is known as bone modeling. Modeling primarily takes place during a bone’s growth. However, in adult life, bone undergoes remodeling, in which resorption of old or damaged bone takes place on the same surface where osteoblasts lay new bone to replace that which is resorbed. Injury, exercise, and other activities lead to remodeling. Those influences are discussed later in the unit, but even without injury or exercise, about 5 to 10 percent of the skeleton is remodeled annually just by destroying old bone and renewing it with fresh bone.

A fracture is a broken bone. It will heal whether or not a physician resets it in its anatomical position. If the bone is not reset correctly, the healing process will keep the bone in its deformed position. 

Fractures are classified by their complexity, location, and other features. Some common types of fractures are shown here. Some fractures may be described using more than one term because it may have the features of more than one type (e.g., an open transverse fracture).

slides.title: Section B Overview

Section B Overview

Skeleton
206 major bones in adults (number is greater during development, as some fuse)
2 divisions:
axial skeleton
appendicular skeleton
must know those in this PPT lecture (including this figure), but not all bones shown in textbook

Axial and Appendicular Skeleton. The axial skeleton supports the head, neck, back, and chest and thus forms the vertical axis of the body. It consists of the skull, vertebral column (including the sacrum and coccyx), and the thoracic cage, formed by the ribs and sternum. The appendicular skeleton is made up of all bones of the upper and lower limbs.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Section B in the textbook contains extensive coverage of the skeletal system. You will not be responsible for learning every bone in the body—such an endeavour would be more appropriate for a laboratory course. Rather, here we will focus on some main structures. The only bones that you are responsible for knowing are those in this diagram (which is Diagram 29 in Unit 10 of the textbook), plus any other bones that are covered in these presentations.

As a reminder, the skeletal system includes all of the bones, cartilages, and ligaments of the body that support and give shape to the body and body structures. The skeleton consists of the bones of the body. For adults, there are 206 major bones in the skeleton. Younger individuals have higher numbers of bones because some bones fuse together during childhood and adolescence to form an adult bone.  The skeleton is subdivided into two major divisions – the axial skeleton and the appendicular skeleton.

attachment site for muscles that move the head, neck, and back
attachment site for muscles that act across the shoulder and hip joints to move their corresponding limbs

Axial and Appendicular Skeleton. The axial skeleton supports the head, neck, back, and chest and thus forms the vertical axis of the body. It consists of the skull, vertebral column (including the sacrum and coccyx), and the thoracic cage, formed by the ribs and sternum. The appendicular skeleton is made up of all bones of the upper and lower limbs.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The axial skeleton forms the vertical, central axis of the body and includes all bones of the head, neck, chest, and back. It serves to protect the brain, spinal cord, heart, and lungs. It also serves as the attachment site for muscles that move the head, neck, and back, and for muscles that act across the shoulder and hip joints to move their corresponding limbs.

Apart form the skull, the head is also associated with several additional bones, including the hyoid bone of the neck and the ear ossicles (three small bones found in each middle ear). The vertebral column consists of numerous bones, each called a vertebra, plus the sacrum and coccyx. The thoracic cage includes many pairs of ribs, most of them anchored anteriorly to the sternum, the flattened bone of the anterior chest. Even though the book states them, you do not need to memorize the number of bones in each section of the body.

Parts of the Skull. The skull consists of the rounded brain case that houses the brain and the facial bones that form the upper and lower jaws, nose, orbits, and other facial structures.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Let’s start our examination of the axial skeleton with the cranium, otherwise known as the skull.

The cranium is subdivided into the facial bones and the brain case, or cranial vault. The facial bones underlie the facial structures, form the nasal cavity, enclose the eyeballs, and support the teeth of the upper and lower jaws. The rounded brain case surrounds and protects the brain and houses the middle and inner ear structures.

The mandible (lower jaw) is the only moveable bone of the skull.

slides.title: Part 1: The Axial Skeleton
slides.body:
Part 1: The Axial Skeleton

The Cranium (Skull)
fontanelles
soft spots of dense connective tissue in fetal skull separating brain case bones
allow skull to change shape as it passes through birth canal
allow for skull enlargement after birth (as brain grows)
decrease in size and disappear by age 2
sutures
dense fibrous connective tissue, uniting cranial bones and allowing for more growth
eventually calcify and harden

Newborn Skull. The bones of the newborn skull are not fully ossified and are separated by large areas called fontanelles, which are filled with fibrous connective tissue. The fontanelles allow for continued growth of the skull after birth. At the time of birth, the facial bones are small and underdeveloped, and the mastoid process has not yet formed.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: As the brain case bones grow in the fetal skull, they remain separated from each other by large areas of dense connective tissue, each of which is called a fontanelle. The fontanelles are the soft spots on an infant’s head. They are important during birth because these areas allow the skull to change shape as it squeezes through the birth canal. After birth, the fontanelles allow for continued growth and expansion of the skull as the brain enlarges. The fontanelles decrease in size and disappear by age 2. However, the skull bones remained separated from each other at the sutures, which contain dense fibrous connective tissue that unites the adjacent bones. The connective tissue of the sutures allows for continued growth of the skull bones as the brain enlarges during childhood growth.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The facial bones of the skull form the upper and lower jaws, the nose, nasal cavity and nasal septum, and the eye orbits. 

The maxillary bone, often referred to simply as the maxilla, is one of a pair that together form the upper jaw.

The mandible forms the lower jaw and is the only moveable bone of the skull.

slides.title: Part 1: The Axial Skeleton
slides.body:
Part 1: The Axial Skeleton

The vertebral column (spine)
consists of vertebrae
each separated by intervertebral disc made of fibrocartilage
supports the head, neck, and body
and allows for their movement 
protects the spinal cord (found inside vertebral openings)

Vertebral Column. The adult vertebral column consists of 24 vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. The vertebrae are divided into three regions: cervical C1–C7 vertebrae, thoracic T1–T12 vertebrae, and lumbar L1–L5 vertebrae. The vertebral column is curved, with two primary curvatures (thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves) and two secondary curvatures (cervical and lumbar curves).

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The vertebral column is also known as the spinal column or spine. It consists of a sequence of vertebrae, each of which is separated and united by an intervertebral disc. It is a flexible column that supports the head, neck, and body and allows for their movements. It also protects the spinal cord, which passes down the back through openings in the vertebrae.

The adult vertebral column consists of 24 vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. The vertebral column is subdivided into five regions, with the vertebrae in each area named for that region and numbered in descending order.

Vertebral Column. The adult vertebral column consists of 24 vertebrae, plus the sacrum and coccyx. The vertebrae are divided into three regions: cervical C1–C7 vertebrae, thoracic T1–T12 vertebrae, and lumbar L1–L5 vertebrae. The vertebral column is curved, with two primary curvatures (thoracic and sacrococcygeal curves) and two secondary curvatures (cervical and lumbar curves).

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In the neck, there are seven cervical vertebrae, each designated with the letter “C” followed by its number. 

Below these are the 12 thoracic vertebrae, designated T1–T12. The ribs are anchored posteriorly to the 12 thoracic vertebrae.

The lower back contains the L1–L5 lumbar vertebrae. 

The single sacrum, which is also part of the pelvis, is formed by the fusion of five sacral vertebrae. 

Similarly, the coccyx, or tailbone, results from the fusion of four small coccygeal vertebrae. However, the sacral and coccygeal fusions do not start until age 20 and are not completed until middle age.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The bones of the appendicular skeleton are divided into two groups: the bones that are located within the limbs themselves, and the girdle bones that attach the limbs to the axial skeleton. The bones of the shoulder region form the pectoral girdle, which anchors the upper limb to the thoracic cage of the axial skeleton. The lower limb is attached to the vertebral column by the pelvic girdle.

Clavicle (top) and Scapula (bottom). Adapted from: Anatomography, CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Pectoral Girdle. The pectoral girdle consists of the clavicle and the scapula, which serve to attach the upper limb to the sternum of the axial skeleton.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The pectoral girdle consists of the clavicle and the scapula.

The clavicle (or collarbone) is an S-shaped bone that connects the sternum of the thoracic cage with the scapula just above the shoulder joint. 

The scapula (or shoulder blade) connects the clavicle to the humerus (or upper arm bone) to form the shoulder joint. 

Both of these bones serve as important attachment sites for muscles that aid with movements of the shoulder and arm.

Upper Limb Bones. Credit: LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The upper limb is divided into three regions. These consist of the arm, located between the shoulder and elbow joints; the forearm, which is between the elbow and wrist joints; and the hand, which is located distal to the wrist. 

The humerus is the single bone of the upper arm, and the ulna (medially) and the radius (laterally) are the paired bones of the forearm. The base of the hand contains the carpal bones, the palm of the hand the metacarpal bones, and the fingers and thumb contain phalanx bones, or phalanges.

Pelvis. Credit: BruceBlaus. Blausen.com staff (2014). "Medical gallery of Blausen Medical 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.010. ISSN 2002-4436., CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The pelvic girdle (or hip girdle) is formed by paired coxal bones or hip bones, which serve as the attachment points for the lower limb. Each hip bone, in turn, is joined to the axial skeleton via its attachment to the sacrum of the vertebral column. The right and left hip bones also converge anteriorly to attach to each other. 

The bony pelvis is the entire structure formed by the two hip bones (the pelvic girdle), and the sacrum plus the coccyx (the pelvic spine).

slides.title: Part 3: The Pelvic Girdle and Pelvis
slides.body:
Part 3: The Pelvic Girdle and Pelvis

Comparison of the female and male pelvis
male
thicker – supports greater male weight and stronger muscles (on average)
narrower – adapted for bipedal locomotion
female
wider – balanced adaptation for childbirth (wide) and locomotion (narrow)
larger subpubic angle due to this width
sacrum is wider, shorter, and tilted back more
pelvic inlet (pelvic brim) more oval compared to males

Male and Female Pelves. The female pelvis is adapted for childbirth and is broader, with a larger subpubic angle, a rounder pelvic brim, and a wider and more shallow lesser pelvic cavity than the male pelvis.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The differences between the adult female and male pelvis relate to function and body size. In general, the bones of the male pelvis are thicker and heavier, adapted to support the male’s heavier physical build and stronger muscles, on average. 

Bipedal movement requires a relatively narrow pelvis, while birth of infants with large brains and thus large heads requires a relatively broad pelvis. Because the female pelvis is adapted for childbirth, it is wider than the male pelvis, although its width is constrained by the need for bipedal locomotion. The latter constrains the pelvic width from being too wide, and makes childbirth challenging, requiring human infants to be born in a relatively underdeveloped state—before their brains and heads have grown too large. As a result, human infants need more parental care than do infants of many other mammalian species. 

Because of this increased pelvic width, the subpubic angle is larger in females than it is in males. The female sacrum is wider, shorter, and tilted back more so that the sacral promontory projects less into the pelvic cavity, thus giving the female pelvic inlet (pelvic brim) a more rounded or oval shape compared to males.

Bones of the Lower Limb

leg

tarsals

Foot Bones. Adapted from: LadyofHats, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Like the upper limb, the lower limb is divided into three regions. 

The thigh is that portion of the lower limb located between the hip joint and knee joint.

The leg is specifically the region between the knee joint and the ankle joint. 

Distal to the ankle is the foot. 

The bones of the lower limb are the femur, patella, tibia, fibula, tarsal bones, metatarsal bones, and phalanges. The femur is the single bone of the thigh. The patella is the kneecap and articulates with the distal femur. The tibia is the larger, weight-bearing bone located on the medial side of the leg, and the fibula is the thin bone of the lateral leg, which aids in ankle-joint stability and movement. 

The bones of the foot are divided into three groups. The posterior portion of the foot is formed by a group of tarsal bones, whereas the mid-foot contains the metatarsal bones, and the toes contain the phalanx bones (or phalanges).
